title: How do fungi eat without a mouth?
group: HOWN — How and Why in Nature

explain.say: Fungi have no mouth and no stomach, and they cannot make food from sunlight like plants. So how do they eat? Let us zoom into the woodland floor to find out.

explain.say: Lift some damp dead leaves and you often see fine white threads. This is mycelium, the feeding body of a fungus, wrapped around everything it can eat.

explain.say: Each thread, or hypha, is so thin it is usually just one cell wide. It grows at its tip, pushing into the food and branching again and again.

explain.say: The tips pour out digestive enzymes that dissolve the food outside the fungus. Then the threads soak up the dissolved sugars and nutrients. Fungi digest first and eat afterwards.

faq.a: Fungi release enzymes from their threads into the food around them. The enzymes break big molecules like cellulose into small ones, which the fungus then absorbs. It is digestion outside the body.
Hyphae are the thin, branching threads that make up a fungus. Together they form the mycelium, and their huge surface lets the fungus absorb food quickly.

faq.q: Why do fungi grow in damp places?
faq.a: Hyphae are thin and soft, so they dry out easily, and their enzymes work in water. Damp places like soil, logs and leaf litter suit them best.
asks: Why is there fungus in wet places?

faq.a: Most fungi feed on dead material such as leaves, wood, dung and fallen fruit. Some live on living plants or animals as parasites, and many team up with plant roots, trading nutrients for sugar.
Yes. Some fungi are among the very few living things that can break down lignin, the tough material in wood. Without them, dead trees would pile up for much longer.

facts: Fungi digest food outside their bodies by releasing enzymes, then absorb the dissolved nutrients.
A single gram of soil can contain many metres of fungal hyphae.
White-rot fungi are among the few organisms that can fully break down lignin in wood.
